The "courses" were not academic classes but the dishes/courses of a banquet meal. The student had been invited to a formal dinner/banquet hosted by someone else (such as a wedding or college high-table dinner), where guests must pre-select their menu choices before an RSVP/meal-choice deadline. The student chose their courses by that deadline and attended the event.

At the banquet, the student was served each course and ate it. After each course was finished, the waiters/staff cleared away the empty plate — the "group" that deliberately "took" the courses was the serving/clearing staff. So by the end of the evening, every course the student had selected had been eaten and its plate removed, giving the impression that "all my courses were gone in one evening." The complaint is a wordplay: the courses vanished simply because the student ate them and the waiters whisked the plates away.

The "courses" are not university classes but the courses/dishes of a meal, and the "deadline" is the deadline for pre-selecting one's menu choices (an RSVP/meal-choice cutoff) for a dinner. The student had to choose their dishes in advance for a multi-course dinner hosted by someone else. On the evening of that dinner, the student attended in person and was served and ate each course they had chosen; once each course was finished, the waiters cleared the plate away.

So "all my courses were gone in one evening" simply describes a normal, satisfactory dinner: the whole multi-course meal was served, eaten and cleared within that single evening. Nothing was stolen or lost—the food was gone because it was a one-evening, sit-down banquet meal that the student consumed and had cleared. The puzzle's misdirection is that "courses" and "deadline" sound like academic course selection, when in fact they refer to the dishes chosen for that dinner.

Is the intended "aha" that the student used academic-sounding words ("courses," "deadline") to describe choosing dishes at a university hall dinner, so the opening misleadingly sounds like class registration?

The trick is a deliberate misdirection in wording. At the University of Hong Kong, the student's hall/college was holding a formal dinner. Before the sign-up/registration deadline, each student had to choose their "courses"—but these were the courses (dishes) of the meal, not academic classes. So "I must choose my courses before the deadline" is really about picking menu dishes for the hall dinner.

The student attended that dinner in person and was served and ate each dish they had chosen. As each course was finished, the waiting staff cleared the empty plate away. By the end of that one evening, the entire multi-course dinner had been served, eaten and cleared—hence "all of my courses were gone in one evening."

It was an ordinary, satisfactory hall dinner: nothing was stolen and the student lost nothing. The "mystery" is only that academic-sounding words ("courses," "deadline") were used to describe the dishes and the meal sign-up cutoff, making a simple dinner sound like a course-registration disaster.

The central trick is a deliberate misdirection in wording. The "courses" were not university classes but the dishes of a meal, and the "deadline" was the sign-up/registration cutoff for a formal dinner held by the student's university hall/college. Students had to pre-select their menu dishes by that deadline.

On the evening of the dinner, the student attended in person and was served the chosen dishes one course after another. Because it was a formal, multi-course dinner, each plate was cleared away to make way for the next course—even though the student had not managed to finish everything on it, leaving some good food uneaten. So course by course the plates were taken away, and by the end of that single evening every course the student had chosen had come and gone.

Thus "all of my courses were gone in one evening" simply describes a normal hall dinner: the whole sequence of courses was served and cleared within that one evening, and the remaining food the student hadn't finished disappeared with the plates. Nothing sinister happened—no one stole the student's food and there was no disaster. The apparent "course-registration catastrophe" is only the misleading use of academic-sounding words ("courses," "deadline") to describe choosing and eating dishes at a hall dinner, with the plates being cleared away by the waiting staff.
